items.stem: A 24-year-old man arrives after a fall from a ladder with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 and a blown right pupil. A head computed tomography scan shows a lens-shaped extra-axial collection. Which finding best identifies this lesion?
options: A crescent hematoma that crosses suture lines, from bridging vein tearing
Blood in the basal cisterns, from a ruptured berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis
Punctate hemorrhages at the gray-white junction, from shear injury
A biconvex hematoma limited by suture lines, from middle meningeal artery injury
items.explanation: An epidural hematoma is a biconvex collection limited by the cranial sutures, classically from a temporal bone fracture that tears the middle meningeal artery. Rapid expansion causes herniation and a dilated ipsilateral pupil, so urgent craniotomy is indicated. A crescent crossing sutures indicates subdural bleeding from bridging veins. Cisternal blood suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage, and punctate gray-white hemorrhages describe diffuse axonal injury.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man has a long history of reflux and a 3-centimeter segment of salmon-colored mucosa above the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsies show intestinal metaplasia with no dysplasia. What is the best management?
options: Perform an esophagectomy now to remove the entire metaplastic segment
Continue acid suppression and schedule endoscopic surveillance
Start chemoradiation therapy for early malignancy
Stop endoscopy because nondysplastic disease never progresses
items.explanation: Barrett esophagus without dysplasia carries a low annual risk of progression to adenocarcinoma, so proton pump inhibitor therapy and periodic surveillance endoscopy with biopsies is recommended. Esophagectomy is excessive for nondysplastic disease. Chemoradiation applies to established cancer, not metaplasia. The risk is low but not zero, so surveillance is retained, and dysplasia or early cancer prompts endoscopic eradication therapy.

items.stem: A 74-year-old woman has three days of left lower quadrant pain and fever. Computed tomography shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 6-centimeter pelvic abscess. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
options: Percutaneous drainage and antibiotics, then colonoscopy and elective resection
Emergent Hartmann procedure for every pelvic abscess regardless of hemodynamic stability
Oral antibiotics alone with early discharge
Laparoscopic lavage without drainage or antibiotics
items.explanation: Hinchey stage II diverticulitis with an abscess larger than about 3 to 4 centimeters is managed with percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics in a stable patient, which often avoids emergency surgery and a stoma. Interval colonoscopy excludes cancer, and elective resection is considered after recovery. Emergency resection is reserved for peritonitis or failed drainage. Oral antibiotics alone rarely clear a large abscess, and lavage alone without antibiotics is inadequate.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has right upper quadrant pain, fever of 39 degrees, jaundice, and confusion with a blood pressure of 85/50 mm Hg. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with a stone. What is the best management?
options: Oral antibiotics and elective cholecystectomy performed next month as an outpatient
Immediate laparoscopic cholecystectomy without any drainage of the biliary tree
Resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and urgent biliary decompression
Observation until liver enzymes normalize
items.explanation: Fever, jaundice, pain, hypotension, and confusion form the five elements of severe acute cholangitis, which is a surgical emergency. Treatment is resuscitation, antibiotics, and urgent decompression of the duct, usually by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with stent or sphincterotomy. Cholecystectomy does not relieve ductal obstruction. Oral therapy is inadequate for septic shock, and waiting for laboratory values to improve risks death.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 41 and untreated snoring is scheduled for an elective hernia repair under general anesthesia. He reports daytime sleepiness and witnessed apneas. Which preoperative step best reduces his risk of postoperative respiratory events?
options: Screen for apnea and plan continuous oximetry with limited opioids
Cancel surgery until a full polysomnogram is completed in every case
Plan routine postoperative sedatives to avoid anxiety-related desaturation
Reassure him because snoring alone carries no anesthetic risk
items.explanation: Suspected obstructive sleep apnea raises the risk of airway obstruction and hypoxemia after anesthesia. Screening tools identify likely cases, and care can proceed with opioid-sparing analgesia, head-up positioning, and continuous oximetry. Mandatory polysomnography delays needed surgery without proven benefit. Sedatives worsen upper airway collapse. Dismissing the symptoms ignores a well-documented perioperative hazard, especially in patients with obesity.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 2-centimeter invasive ductal carcinoma that is strongly estrogen receptor positive, HER2 negative, and clinically node negative. She wishes to preserve her breast. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Mastectomy with full axillary dissection in every case of invasive carcinoma
Chemotherapy alone with no surgery
Radiation to the chest wall only after observation
Lumpectomy with sentinel node biopsy, radiation, and endocrine therapy
items.explanation: A small node-negative invasive carcinoma suits breast conservation, since survival after lumpectomy with radiation is equivalent to mastectomy. Sentinel node biopsy stages the axilla with less morbidity than full dissection. Endocrine therapy lowers recurrence for receptor-positive tumors. Mastectomy with routine dissection is excessive here. Chemotherapy alone does not remove the tumor, and radiation without resection leaves gross disease in place.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with a small bowel fistula has lost large volumes of fluid for days. Serum sodium is 129 mEq per liter, and he is dry with a low urine sodium. Which finding on laboratory testing best matches this state?
options: Euvolemic hyponatremia with a urine sodium above 40 mEq per liter
Hypovolemic hyponatremia with a urine sodium below 20 mEq per liter
Hypervolemic hyponatremia with a markedly high urine osmolality
Hypernatremia from free water loss with a high serum osmolality
items.explanation: Extrarenal loss of isotonic fluid with replacement by free water produces hypovolemic hyponatremia, and the kidney conserves sodium, so urine sodium falls below 20. Euvolemic states such as inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion show high urine sodium. Hypervolemic hyponatremia occurs in heart, liver, or kidney failure with edema. Hypernatremia would need predominant water loss, which does not fit a gut fistula replaced with water.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a 2.2-millimeter thick melanoma of the back without ulceration and no palpable nodes. What is the recommended surgical margin and nodal evaluation?
options: Excision with a 5-millimeter margin and no nodal assessment
Excision with a 5-centimeter margin and routine elective lymph node dissection
Wide local excision with a 2-centimeter margin and sentinel lymph node biopsy
Mohs surgery with observation of the nodal basins
items.explanation: For melanoma thicker than 2 millimeters, a 2-centimeter margin is standard, and sentinel node biopsy is recommended for intermediate-thickness tumors because nodal status is the strongest predictor of outcome. A 5-millimeter margin applies to in situ disease. Wider margins beyond 2 centimeters add morbidity without benefit, and elective dissection without a positive sentinel node is unnecessary. Mohs surgery is not the standard for invasive melanoma.

items.stem: A 28-year-old man develops fever, a diffuse erythematous rash, hypotension, and diarrhea on day 3 after nasal packing for bleeding. The packing is removed. Which treatment combination is most appropriate?
options: Oral corticosteroids alone with close outpatient observation at home
A single dose of a narrow-spectrum penicillin only
Immediate surgical debridement of the nasal mucosa
Fluid resuscitation plus clindamycin to suppress toxin production
items.explanation: Toxic shock syndrome results from superantigen exotoxins that activate large numbers of T cells. Treatment is source removal, aggressive volume resuscitation, and antibiotics active against staphylococci and streptococci, with clindamycin added to suppress toxin synthesis. Steroids alone and observation are inadequate for shock. A single narrow antibiotic dose does not halt toxin production. Debridement is reserved for necrotizing soft tissue infection, which is not described.

items.stem: A 70-year-old man has sudden severe pain in his right foot, which is pale, cold, and paralyzed with absent sensation. He has atrial fibrillation and is not anticoagulated. Pulses are absent below the femoral level. What is the best immediate management?
options: Elevate the limb and wait for the pain to resolve overnight in the ward
Start anticoagulation and proceed urgently to revascularization
Schedule an outpatient angiogram for the next available week in clinic
Apply warm compresses and give oral analgesics
items.explanation: Acute limb ischemia from an embolus with sensory loss and motor paralysis is a threatened limb, Rutherford class III, and requires immediate anticoagulation to stop propagation, then embolectomy, thrombolysis, or bypass within hours. Irreversible muscle necrosis occurs after about 6 hours of complete ischemia. Elevation reduces perfusion, delayed imaging risks amputation, and warming an ischemic limb increases metabolic demand and offers no benefit.

items.stem: A 3-week-old firstborn boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry afterward. He is dehydrated, and an olive-shaped mass is palpable in the epigastrium. Which metabolic derangement is expected, and what is the first step?
options: Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, corrected after pyloromyotomy
Hyperkalemic metabolic acidosis, corrected with insulin first
Hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, corrected before pyloromyotomy
Normal electrolytes, with surgery performed urgently
items.explanation: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium, leading to hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, with paradoxical aciduria as the kidney conserves sodium. The infant is resuscitated with isotonic fluid and potassium until chloride and bicarbonate normalize, since anesthesia in an alkalotic infant risks apnea. Pyloromyotomy is then curative. The other patterns do not fit persistent vomiting of gastric contents.

items.stem: A trial compares a new mesh with standard mesh for hernia repair. Recurrence occurs in 4 percent with the new mesh and 8 percent with standard mesh. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one recurrence?
options: Twenty-five patients, from an absolute risk reduction of 4 percentage points
Twelve patients, from the reciprocal of the control recurrence rate of 8 percent
Fifty patients, from the relative risk reduction
Four patients, from the recurrence rate of the new mesh
items.explanation: Number needed to treat equals one divided by the absolute risk reduction. The absolute risk reduction is 8 percent minus 4 percent, or 0.04, so the number needed to treat is 25. Using the control rate alone gives 12, which ignores the treatment effect. The relative risk reduction is 50 percent and is not the denominator. Reporting the treated rate as the answer confuses an event rate with a reciprocal.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman is struck while crossing a street. She has a pulse of 118, blood pressure of 92/60 mm Hg, and a positive pelvic compression finding with perineal bruising. Free fluid is absent on ultrasound. Which is the best initial step to control pelvic hemorrhage?
options: Log-roll repeatedly to test pelvic stability at the bedside
Insert a urinary catheter before any other maneuver
Apply a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters and begin balanced transfusion
Start a large crystalloid bolus and hold the binder until computed tomography is done
items.explanation: Unstable pelvic ring fractures bleed from venous plexuses and fracture surfaces, so rapid volume reduction with a binder centered on the greater trochanters, together with blood product resuscitation, comes first. Repeated stress testing dislodges clots. A catheter is deferred when perineal bruising suggests urethral injury. Large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and worsen bleeding. Angioembolization or preperitoneal packing follows if she remains unstable.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and a 9-kilogram weight loss. A barium study shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth narrowing at the gastroesophageal junction. Which test is required before any treatment?
options: Upper endoscopy with biopsy to exclude a malignancy mimicking achalasia
Twenty-four-hour pH monitoring to quantify acid exposure
Gastric emptying scintigraphy to assess outlet obstruction
Serum gastrin level with a secretin stimulation test
items.explanation: Older age, short symptom duration, and marked weight loss raise concern for pseudoachalasia, in which a tumor at the gastroesophageal junction produces the same radiographic picture. Endoscopy with biopsy, often with endoscopic ultrasound, must precede myotomy or dilation. High-resolution manometry then confirms the diagnosis. Acid monitoring, gastric emptying, and gastrin testing address reflux, gastroparesis, and gastrinoma, none of which explain this obstruction.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has bright red blood per rectum and a 2-centimeter polyp removed at colonoscopy. Pathology shows a villous adenoma with high-grade dysplasia and no invasion. Which surveillance interval is most appropriate after complete removal?
options: Repeat colonoscopy in ten years as for average-risk screening
Repeat colonoscopy in three years because the adenoma was advanced
Annual fecal immunochemical testing alone indefinitely
No further surveillance because the lesion was fully removed at colonoscopy
items.explanation: Adenomas that are advanced, meaning large, villous, or with high-grade dysplasia, signal a higher risk of new neoplasia and call for a shorter interval, generally three years after complete removal. A ten-year interval applies after a normal examination or a few small adenomas. Stool testing alone is insufficient for a patient with a known advanced adenoma, and no surveillance ignores the field defect that produced the polyp.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman has painless jaundice and a palpable, nontender gallbladder. Computed tomography shows a 2.5-centimeter pancreatic head mass abutting the superior mesenteric vein for less than 180 degrees without arterial involvement. What is the best next step?
options: Immediate palliative bypass without any tissue diagnosis or staging
Radiation therapy alone to the pancreatic head
Routine preoperative stenting in every patient with obstructive jaundice and no delay
Staging for resectability, with stenting only for cholangitis or delayed surgery
items.explanation: A pancreatic head mass with limited venous contact and no arterial encasement may be resectable or borderline, and the first step is complete staging and multidisciplinary review. The Courvoisier sign reflects distal biliary obstruction. Stenting is reserved for cholangitis, severe pruritus, or delayed surgery because routine stenting raises infectious complications. Palliative bypass and radiation alone forgo a potentially curative resection.

items.stem: A 72-year-old woman with a recent drug-eluting coronary stent placed 3 weeks ago needs an urgent but not emergent cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis recovery. She takes aspirin and clopidogrel. What is the best antiplatelet strategy?
options: Stop both antiplatelet agents a week before the operation
Continue aspirin and coordinate any pause of the second agent with cardiology
Stop aspirin but continue only the second agent through surgery
Replace both agents with a prophylactic anticoagulant until the day of surgery
items.explanation: Stent thrombosis risk is highest in the first weeks after placement, and stopping dual therapy early carries a high rate of myocardial infarction. Aspirin is generally continued perioperatively, and elective surgery is deferred when possible. If surgery cannot wait, the cardiologist and surgeon decide jointly about the second agent. Stopping both drugs invites thrombosis, and substituting an anticoagulant does not protect a stent.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman has a bloody unilateral nipple discharge from a single duct. Mammography and ultrasound are normal. Which diagnosis is most likely, and what is the best management?
options: Fibrocystic change, with observation of the discharge
Duct ectasia, with antibiotics for an assumed ductal infection
Intraductal papilloma, with excision of the involved duct
Paget disease, with topical steroid cream
items.explanation: Spontaneous, unilateral, single-duct bloody discharge is most often caused by an intraductal papilloma, though a small proportion hide carcinoma, so surgical duct excision provides the diagnosis. Fibrocystic changes and duct ectasia typically cause multiduct, green or brown discharge in older or premenopausal women. Paget disease is an eczematous nipple change with underlying carcinoma, and steroid cream would delay diagnosis.

items.stem: A 62-year-old woman on postoperative day 4 after total gastrectomy has an ileus, minimal oral intake, and a new weakness. She has been on parenteral nutrition for three days. Which laboratory change signals refeeding syndrome?
options: Rising serum phosphate with falling serum calcium
Rising serum potassium with metabolic acidosis
Falling serum sodium with rising blood urea nitrogen
Falling serum phosphate, potassium, and magnesium after nutrition is restarted
items.explanation: Reintroducing carbohydrate to a starved patient raises insulin, which drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells and lowers their serum levels. Low phosphate causes weakness, respiratory failure, and arrhythmia. Thiamine should be given before feeding is advanced, and calories are increased slowly. Hyperphosphatemia and hyperkalemia suggest renal failure instead, and dilutional sodium change with azotemia reflects volume status, not this intracellular shift.

items.stem: A 60-year-old woman has a 7-centimeter deep, firm, enlarging mass in the thigh. Magnetic resonance imaging suggests a soft tissue sarcoma, and core needle biopsy confirms a high-grade tumor. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
options: Limb-sparing wide excision with radiation therapy, planned by a sarcoma team
Simple enucleation of the mass through a short incision
Amputation of the limb as first-line therapy
Chemotherapy alone with no resection
items.explanation: High-grade extremity sarcoma larger than 5 centimeters is treated with wide excision to negative margins combined with radiation, preserving the limb with outcomes equivalent to amputation. Biopsy is placed along the planned incision. Enucleation leaves microscopic disease and raises local recurrence. Amputation is reserved for tumors that cannot be cleared by limb-sparing surgery. Chemotherapy is an adjunct for selected tumors and does not replace resection.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man has a hemoglobin of 7.4 grams per deciliter before a planned colectomy. He has a mean corpuscular volume of 72, low ferritin, and guaiac-positive stool. What is the best preoperative strategy?
options: Proceed directly to surgery and give prophylactic transfusion of two red cell units
Give erythropoietin alone without checking iron stores
Defer surgery for six months and recheck only the hemoglobin
Find the source of blood loss and give iron, transfusing only if symptomatic
items.explanation: A microcytic picture with low ferritin indicates iron deficiency from chronic gastrointestinal loss, which a colon lesion explains. Iron repletion, oral or intravenous, improves hemoglobin and is preferred over reflex transfusion, which carries risk and is reserved for symptomatic or unstable anemia. Erythropoietin without iron is ineffective. A prolonged delay for a lesion needing resection is unnecessary when iron can be given over weeks.

items.stem: A 66-year-old woman has a 5.8-centimeter infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm found incidentally, with no symptoms. She is a good operative candidate with a normal life expectancy. What is the best recommendation?
options: Repeat ultrasonography in 12 months without intervention
Beta-blocker therapy alone to prevent growth
Elective repair, either open or endovascular, based on anatomy
Emergency laparotomy tonight
items.explanation: Repair is recommended when an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm reaches about 5.5 centimeters in men and somewhat smaller in women, since rupture risk then outweighs operative risk. Anatomy determines open versus endovascular repair. Surveillance suits smaller aneurysms. Medical therapy does not reliably halt growth, and emergent surgery is for rupture or symptoms, not an incidental finding in a stable patient who can be planned electively.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has a 2-centimeter lung nodule with spiculated margins found on chest radiograph. He has a 40 pack-year smoking history and a normal lung function study. Positron emission tomography shows avid uptake in the nodule only, with no nodal or distant disease. What is the best treatment?
options: Wedge resection without nodal sampling in all patients
Anatomic resection by lobectomy with mediastinal lymph node sampling
Primary chemotherapy followed by observation
Surveillance imaging every six months for two years
items.explanation: A stage I non-small cell lung cancer in a fit patient is treated by lobectomy with systematic lymph node sampling, which gives lower local recurrence than limited resection. A suspicious spiculated nodule with positron emission uptake should not be observed. Chemotherapy first is not indicated for stage I disease. Wedge resection is reserved for patients with limited reserve, and stereotactic radiation is used for those who cannot tolerate surgery.

items.stem: A 78-year-old man with advanced dementia and a perforated viscus is unable to communicate. His adult daughter says he never wanted aggressive care, but he has no written directive. Who should decide, and on what basis?
options: The surrogate decision maker, applying what the patient would have chosen
The operating surgeon alone, applying a standard of maximal treatment to all patients
The hospital administrator, applying institutional policy
The most distant relative, applying personal preference
items.explanation: When a patient lacks capacity and has no directive, a surrogate, usually a close family member according to local law, decides using substituted judgment, meaning what the patient would have wanted, and otherwise the patient's best interest. The surgeon provides information and recommendations but does not decide alone. Administrators do not make individual treatment decisions, and relatives chosen by distance rather than relationship have no standing.

items.stem: A 40-year-old man has a stab wound to the right neck at the angle of the mandible, with an expanding hematoma, stridor, and active bleeding. Which neck zone is involved, and what is the appropriate management?
options: Zone 1, with delayed observation in a monitored bed
Zone 3, with initial treatment by angiography alone
Zone 2, with immediate airway control and operative exploration for the unstable patient
Zone 2, with discharge after a normal chest radiograph
items.explanation: Zone 2 spans the cricoid cartilage to the angle of the mandible and is the most accessible to surgical exploration. A patient with a hard sign such as an expanding hematoma, active bleeding, or airway compromise goes directly to the operating room after securing the airway. Zone 1 and zone 3 injuries more often require imaging or endovascular planning for exposure. Observation and discharge are inappropriate with hard signs.

items.stem: A 45-year-old man develops epigastric pain, early satiety, and an episode of melena. Endoscopy shows a 2-centimeter duodenal ulcer, and biopsies are negative for Helicobacter pylori. He takes naproxen daily. What is the most appropriate therapy?
options: Perform a truncal vagotomy and pyloroplasty on an elective basis
Stop the anti-inflammatory drug and give a proton pump inhibitor
Continue the drug and add an antacid taken at bedtime
Give triple eradication therapy despite negative biopsies
items.explanation: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs impair mucosal protection and are a leading cause of duodenal ulcer when infection is absent. Removing the offending drug and giving a proton pump inhibitor heals most ulcers, and repeat testing is reasonable because biopsies after bleeding or acid suppression can be falsely negative. Elective vagotomy is rarely needed. Continuing the drug invites recurrence, and eradication therapy treats an infection that is not shown.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has severe pain with defecation, small amounts of bright red blood, and a sentinel tag. Examination shows a posterior midline fissure with exposed internal sphincter fibers that has persisted for four months despite fiber. What is the best next treatment?
options: Fistulotomy of the posterior midline tract with primary closure of the wound
Rubber band ligation of the internal hemorrhoid
Wide local excision with a diverting colostomy
Topical calcium channel blocker, with sphincterotomy if it fails
items.explanation: Chronic anal fissures are maintained by internal sphincter hypertonia and poor blood flow to the posterior midline. Topical agents relax the sphincter and heal many fissures, and lateral internal sphincterotomy is the most effective surgery when medical therapy fails, with a small risk of incontinence. Fistulotomy treats a fistula, banding treats hemorrhoids, and a colostomy is far beyond what a benign fissure requires.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman has a 6-centimeter well-circumscribed liver lesion found incidentally. She has used oral contraceptives for 12 years. Magnetic resonance imaging shows a heterogeneous lesion with intralesional fat and no central scar. What is the best recommendation?
options: Stop the hormonal contraceptive and consider resection for size and bleeding risk
Continue the contraceptive and repeat the imaging only after five full years have passed
Start systemic chemotherapy for presumed hepatocellular carcinoma
Open liver biopsy as the only step before any decision
items.explanation: Hepatic adenoma is linked to estrogen exposure, contains fat, and lacks the central scar of focal nodular hyperplasia. Lesions over 5 centimeters carry a risk of rupture and rarely of malignant change, so hormone withdrawal and resection are advised. Continuing the estrogen with long delays is unsafe. Chemotherapy is unwarranted without evidence of carcinoma, and percutaneous biopsy risks hemorrhage and seeding and seldom changes management.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman develops fever, muscle rigidity, tachycardia, and rising end-tidal carbon dioxide during induction with succinylcholine and a volatile agent. Her temperature climbs quickly. Which drug is the specific treatment?
options: Bromocriptine given by nasogastric tube
Cyproheptadine given by nasogastric tube
Naloxone given as repeated intravenous boluses
Dantrolene given intravenously after stopping the triggering agents
items.explanation: This is malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis of skeletal muscle triggered by succinylcholine and volatile anesthetics. Dantrolene blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, and treatment also includes stopping triggers, hyperventilation with oxygen, and active cooling. Bromocriptine is used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome, cyproheptadine for serotonin syndrome, and naloxone reverses opioids. None of those stops the muscle hypermetabolism seen here.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has a 1.2-centimeter thyroid nodule with a fine-needle aspiration result of follicular neoplasm, a normal thyrotropin level, and no suspicious nodes. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Diagnostic lobectomy, because invasion cannot be assessed on cytology
Repeat aspiration every year without any surgical intervention
Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection performed immediately
Radioactive iodine ablation without surgery
items.explanation: Cytology cannot distinguish follicular adenoma from carcinoma, because malignancy is defined by capsular or vascular invasion on the final specimen. Diagnostic lobectomy provides that answer with the least morbidity and preserves thyroid function in most patients. Repeated aspiration does not resolve the question. Total thyroidectomy with neck dissection is excessive before a diagnosis. Radioactive iodine ablation requires thyroid tissue removal first and is not a diagnostic tool.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman has a pH of 7.28, bicarbonate of 14 mEq per liter, sodium 140, chloride 116, and a normal serum lactate, after two weeks of high pancreatic fistula output. Which diagnosis best explains the acid-base disturbance?
options: Anion gap metabolic acidosis from unmeasured ketone accumulation
Non-anion gap acidosis from bicarbonate loss in pancreatic secretions
Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation with renal bicarbonate compensation
Metabolic alkalosis from loss of gastric hydrochloric acid
items.explanation: Pancreatic juice is rich in bicarbonate, so prolonged fistula loss lowers serum bicarbonate and the kidney retains chloride, giving a normal anion gap (here 10). Ketoacidosis and lactic acidosis widen the gap, and the lactate is normal. Respiratory acidosis would show a high carbon dioxide with elevated bicarbonate. Metabolic alkalosis follows gastric acid loss, not pancreatic bicarbonate loss. Replacement uses a bicarbonate-containing fluid.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a gastrointestinal stromal tumor of the stomach, 8 centimeters, with a high mitotic rate and a KIT mutation. It is completely resected. What is the best adjuvant approach?
options: No adjuvant therapy because the tumor was resected
Standard doxorubicin-based chemotherapy
Adjuvant imatinib for a defined period
Pelvic radiation after wound healing
items.explanation: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors are driven by KIT or PDGFRA mutations and respond poorly to conventional chemotherapy and radiation. Large size and high mitotic rate mark a high risk of recurrence, and adjuvant imatinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, improves recurrence-free and overall survival, typically for several years. Observation alone is insufficient in high-risk cases. Lymphadenectomy is not required because nodal spread is rare.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman with a history of deep venous thrombosis has a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time that does not correct on mixing with normal plasma. She has no bleeding history. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with a lupus anticoagulant
Hemophilia A with a deficiency of factor VIII
Von Willebrand disease with reduced factor VIII binding
Vitamin K deficiency with reduced factor VII levels
items.explanation: A prolonged aPTT that fails to correct with mixing indicates an inhibitor, and a lupus anticoagulant paradoxically causes clotting, not bleeding, which fits her thrombosis history. Hemophilia and von Willebrand disease give prolonged times that correct with normal plasma and cause bleeding. Vitamin K deficiency prolongs the prothrombin time first and also corrects on mixing. Long-term anticoagulation is generally recommended after thrombosis.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman received a kidney transplant 10 days ago. She now has fever, graft tenderness, a rise in creatinine, and decreasing urine output. Tacrolimus level is therapeutic, and ultrasound shows normal flow without hydronephrosis. What is the next step?
options: Immediate graft nephrectomy to prevent sepsis
Reduction of tacrolimus to prevent toxicity
Percutaneous graft biopsy to diagnose acute rejection and guide immunosuppression
Empiric dialysis catheter placement without further workup
items.explanation: A rising creatinine and tender graft with normal vascular flow and no obstruction suggests acute rejection in the early period. Biopsy distinguishes cellular from antibody-mediated rejection and calcineurin toxicity, which guides treatment with steroids, antithymocyte globulin, or plasma exchange. Nephrectomy is premature. A therapeutic drug level argues against toxicity, so dose reduction would worsen rejection. Dialysis may be needed but does not diagnose the cause.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man has acute onset of severe left scrotal pain with nausea. The testis is high-riding and horizontal, with an absent cremasteric reflex. Doppler ultrasound is not immediately available. What is the best management?
options: Antibiotics for epididymitis and outpatient follow-up
Scrotal elevation and anti-inflammatory therapy at home
Delay until ultrasound can be performed tomorrow
Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
items.explanation: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency, because salvage rates fall steeply after about 6 hours of ischemia. Clinical findings of a high horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex justify exploration without waiting for imaging. The contralateral testis is fixed because the bell clapper anomaly is usually bilateral. Epididymitis therapy, elevation, and delay all risk loss of the testis and are inappropriate with this presentation.

items.stem: In a randomized trial of a new wound dressing, surgical site infection occurred in 12 percent of patients with the standard dressing and 8 percent with the new dressing. Approximately how many patients must receive the new dressing to prevent one infection?
options: About four patients, the absolute risk reduction
About twenty-five patients
About eight patients, the infection rate with the new dressing
About twelve patients, the infection rate with the standard dressing
items.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 12 percent minus 8 percent, or 4 percent, which is 0.04. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal, one divided by 0.04, giving 25. The relative risk reduction would be one third, but that figure does not give the treatment burden. The other values come from confusing the event rates or the relative reduction with the absolute difference.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man in the intensive care unit on day 8 of mechanical ventilation has new fever, purulent secretions, and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Which approach to diagnosis and therapy best reflects current practice?
options: Treat only after a bronchoscopic biopsy confirms the organism
Give a short course of oral antibiotics without any cultures
Obtain lower airway cultures and start empiric therapy for resistant pathogens
Withhold antibiotics and observe because the chest film may be unreliable here
items.explanation: Ventilator-associated pneumonia presents after 48 hours of intubation with new infiltrate, fever, and purulence. Cultures from the lower airway should be sent, but therapy should not wait, and empiric coverage targets resistant gram-negative organisms and methicillin-resistant staphylococci according to local patterns and risk factors. Therapy is narrowed when results return. Waiting for biopsy delays treatment, oral drugs are inadequate, and observation risks progression to sepsis.

items.stem: A 28-year-old woman with recurrent intermittent crampy abdominal pain and a prior appendectomy presents with bilious vomiting and distention. Computed tomography shows dilated small bowel with a transition point and no free fluid, mesenteric swirling, or wall thickening. What is the best initial management?
options: Immediate laparotomy because a transition point always means strangulation
Discharge on a clear liquid diet with oral analgesics and clinic review
Colonoscopic decompression of the small bowel through the terminal ileum
Decompression, fluid resuscitation, and serial examinations with contrast
items.explanation: Adhesive small bowel obstruction is the most common cause after prior abdominal surgery. Without signs of strangulation such as peritonitis, free fluid, wall ischemia, or a closed loop, nonoperative management with decompression, resuscitation, and monitoring succeeds in many patients. Water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution and can be therapeutic. Immediate surgery is for ischemia or failure to progress. Discharge is unsafe, and colonoscopy does not reach the small intestine.

items.stem: A 59-year-old man has a rectal adenocarcinoma 6 centimeters from the anal verge. Staging magnetic resonance imaging shows invasion through the muscularis propria with enlarged mesorectal nodes and a threatened circumferential margin. What is the best initial management?
options: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation followed by total mesorectal excision
Immediate abdominoperineal resection without further staging
Transanal local excision alone with margin clearance
Adjuvant chemotherapy alone after a diverting ileostomy
items.explanation: A locally advanced mid rectal cancer with node involvement or a threatened margin is treated with neoadjuvant chemoradiation, which shrinks tumor, improves margin clearance, and lowers local recurrence, followed by total mesorectal excision. Local excision suits only selected early lesions. Immediate radical surgery without downstaging raises the risk of a positive margin. Chemotherapy alone does not control pelvic disease.

items.stem: A 57-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic viral hepatitis has a single 3-centimeter hepatocellular carcinoma. His bilirubin is normal, he has no ascites, and his portal pressure is not elevated. Which treatment offers the best chance of cure?
options: Systemic chemotherapy as the first-line curative therapy for this stage
Resection, or transplantation if portal hypertension develops
External beam radiation of the whole liver
Observation with alpha-fetoprotein checks and imaging every year
items.explanation: A solitary small tumor in a patient with preserved liver function and no portal hypertension is a good candidate for curative resection. Patients with decompensation or portal hypertension are better served by transplantation within accepted tumor criteria, and ablation is an option for small tumors. Systemic therapy is for advanced disease and is not curative. Whole-liver radiation is toxic, and annual observation lets a curable tumor progress.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has a hemoglobin A1c of 9.8 percent and is scheduled for elective colon resection in two weeks. He asks whether surgery should proceed. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Delay if feasible, since poor control raises infection and leak risk
Proceed unchanged because glycemic control affects only wound healing
Start high-dose corticosteroids to prevent perioperative adrenal crisis
Hold all insulin and glucose monitoring on the day of surgery
items.explanation: Markedly elevated glycated hemoglobin predicts surgical site infection, anastomotic complications, and longer stay, so elective cases are often deferred for optimization when the delay is safe. Perioperative glucose is then targeted in a moderate range. Steroids worsen hyperglycemia and are unnecessary here. Withholding glucose monitoring and basal insulin risks ketoacidosis. The effect of poor control extends beyond the wound to the whole recovery.

items.stem: A 71-year-old man develops a firm 3-centimeter painless neck mass at level II. Fine-needle aspiration shows squamous cell carcinoma. He smokes and has no visible mucosal lesion on office examination. What is the best next step?
options: Excision of the node alone without any further workup
Observation for three months to see if the mass regresses
Panendoscopy with directed biopsies and imaging to find the primary site
Total thyroidectomy as the next step
items.explanation: A solitary lateral neck node containing squamous cell carcinoma in an older smoker is metastatic until proven otherwise, usually from the oropharynx, larynx, or hypopharynx. Evaluation includes cross-sectional imaging, positron emission tomography, and panendoscopy with directed biopsies, often with tonsillectomy and tongue base biopsies. Excisional biopsy alone spreads disease, observation delays care, and thyroidectomy is irrelevant because thyroid cancer is rarely squamous.

items.stem: A 63-year-old woman with small cell lung cancer is admitted with confusion. Serum sodium is 118 mEq per liter, serum osmolality 248 mOsm per kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm per kg, and urine sodium 62 mEq per liter. She appears euvolemic, and thyroid and adrenal function are normal. Which is the best initial management for this chronic, mildly symptomatic hyponatremia?
options: Rapid infusion of isotonic saline to normalize sodium within a few hours and relieve symptoms
Free water loading to dilute the urine
Immediate infusion of hypotonic saline with a loop diuretic
Fluid restriction, with hypertonic saline reserved for severe neurologic symptoms
items.explanation: Concentrated urine with high urinary sodium in a euvolemic patient with a lung tumor indicates inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Fluid restriction is first-line for chronic disease, and correction should stay slow to avoid osmotic demyelination. Isotonic saline can worsen the problem because the solute is excreted while free water is retained. Water loading and hypotonic fluids deepen the dilution.

items.stem: A 68-year-old man has a rapidly growing, 1.5-centimeter violaceous nodule on the cheek that is firm and nontender. Biopsy shows small round blue cells with neuroendocrine markers. What is the most important component of initial surgical management?
options: Narrow excision alone with no evaluation of the regional lymph nodes
Wide excision with sentinel node biopsy and consideration of radiation
Curettage and electrodesiccation in the office setting as definitive therapy
Topical immune therapy applied to the lesion
items.explanation: Merkel cell carcinoma is an aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer linked to polyomavirus and sun exposure, which often spreads to regional nodes early. Wide excision with margins of 1 to 2 centimeters and sentinel node biopsy are standard, and radiation improves local control. Narrow excision invites recurrence. Curettage and topical therapy are for superficial basal and squamous lesions and cannot be used for this high-risk tumor.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man develops fever and chills 30 minutes after beginning a red cell transfusion for postoperative anemia. He has no respiratory distress, his blood pressure is stable, and there is no hemoglobin in his urine. What is the best next step?
options: Continue the transfusion at a faster rate to finish it
Give diuretic therapy and place him on a ventilator for respiratory protection
Stop the transfusion, recheck identification, and give an antipyretic
Start high-dose corticosteroids and a vasopressor infusion
items.explanation: A febrile nonhemolytic reaction is the most common transfusion reaction, caused by recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte cytokines. Because a hemolytic reaction can look identical early, the transfusion is stopped and clerical checks and laboratory review are done. Antipyretics treat the fever, and later products may be leukoreduced. Rapid continuation risks harm if hemolysis exists. Diuresis suits volume overload, and pressors suit anaphylaxis or septic reactions.

items.stem: A 69-year-old man who smokes has an incidentally discovered 5.8 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. He is asymptomatic, has good functional status, and has favorable anatomy. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat ultrasound surveillance in six months
Beta-blocker therapy and imaging in two years
Repair only if he develops back pain
Elective repair, either open or endovascular
items.explanation: Elective repair is advised for asymptomatic aneurysms of at least 5.5 cm in men because rupture risk then outweighs operative risk. Fitness and anatomy allow open repair or endovascular repair, which carries lower early mortality. Surveillance suits smaller aneurysms, and beta-blockers do not meaningfully limit growth. Waiting for symptoms risks rupture, which carries very high mortality.

items.stem: A 5-week-old firstborn boy has projectile nonbilious vomiting after every feeding but remains hungry. He is lethargic with sunken fontanelle, and an olive-shaped mass is felt in the epigastrium. Which set of laboratory findings is most expected?
options: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria
Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia
Hypochloremic metabolic acidosis with hypernatremia
Normal electrolytes with mild respiratory alkalosis
items.explanation: Pyloric stenosis causes loss of gastric hydrochloric acid and potassium, producing hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Volume depletion drives renal sodium retention at the expense of hydrogen, causing paradoxical aciduria. Surgery is delayed until fluids and electrolytes are corrected, then pyloromyotomy is performed. Acidosis patterns suggest other causes such as sepsis or obstruction below the ampulla.

items.stem: A 47-year-old woman with a bleeding gastric ulcer and hemoglobin of 5.8 g/dL tells the team she will not accept blood products because of her religious beliefs. She is alert, understands the risks, and repeats her wishes consistently. What is the most appropriate course?
options: Transfuse anyway under emergency doctrine because the ulcer bleeding is clearly life threatening
Respect her refusal and use all acceptable measures such as endoscopic hemostasis and iron
Obtain a court order before any further treatment
Delay care until a family member agrees to transfusion
items.explanation: An adult with decision-making capacity may refuse treatment, including life-saving transfusion, after informed discussion. The team documents the conversation, then offers every acceptable alternative: endoscopic hemostasis, acid suppression, iron, erythropoiesis stimulation, and minimizing blood draws. Overriding her wishes violates autonomy. A court order is unnecessary without incapacity, and family members cannot override a capable patient.

items.stem: A 19-year-old man is brought in after a motor vehicle crash with a widened mediastinum, a left first rib fracture, and an apical cap on chest radiograph. He is stable. Which test best evaluates the suspected injury?
options: Computed tomographic angiography of the chest to look for aortic injury
Transthoracic echocardiography alone to exclude all vascular injury
Esophagography with water-soluble contrast first
Repeat chest radiography in six hours and discharge if unchanged
items.explanation: A widened mediastinum after high-energy deceleration suggests blunt aortic injury, most often at the ligamentum arteriosum just beyond the left subclavian origin. In a stable patient, computed tomographic angiography is the standard screening and diagnostic study, and treatment is usually endovascular repair with blood pressure control. Echocardiography misses many tears, esophagography addresses a different injury, and delayed repeat films risk a missed lethal lesion.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man with episodic flushing, watery diarrhea, and wheezing has a 3-centimeter ileal mass with liver metastases on imaging. Which urinary test supports the diagnosis?
options: Elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid excretion in a timed sample
Elevated urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid excretion
Elevated urinary free cortisol excretion
Elevated urinary porphobilinogen excretion
items.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome arises when a metastatic neuroendocrine tumor, usually with liver involvement, releases serotonin beyond hepatic inactivation. Serotonin is metabolized to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, which is measured in urine. Vanillylmandelic acid indicates pheochromocytoma, urinary free cortisol indicates Cushing syndrome, and porphobilinogen indicates acute porphyria. Somatostatin analogues relieve symptoms, and resection of the primary and accessible metastases can prolong survival.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a painful bulge at a prior midline laparotomy incision. She has had nausea for 10 hours. Examination shows a firm, tender, irreducible mass with overlying erythema. What is the correct management?
options: Attempted prolonged manual reduction at the bedside
Elective repair after weight loss and outpatient review
Urgent operative repair with assessment of bowel viability
Binder placement and observation for 24 hours
items.explanation: An incarcerated incisional hernia with tenderness, erythema, and obstructive symptoms threatens strangulation, so urgent repair with inspection of the contents and resection of nonviable bowel is required. Forceful reduction can push ischemic bowel back into the abdomen. Elective timing and observation are for asymptomatic or easily reducible hernias. A binder offers no protection against bowel ischemia and delays definitive care.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has nausea, vomiting, and severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Lipase is five times normal, and he has gallstones on ultrasound with a normal bile duct and no cholangitis. When should cholecystectomy be performed?
options: Never, because gallstones are not a cause of recurrent pancreatitis episodes
After six months to allow complete resolution of inflammation
Emergently within hours regardless of severity
During the same admission once the pancreatitis settles, in mild disease
items.explanation: In mild gallstone pancreatitis the risk of recurrent attacks is substantial, so cholecystectomy during the index admission after clinical improvement lowers recurrence and readmission. In severe disease with collections, surgery is delayed until inflammation resolves. Waiting six months leaves the patient exposed to recurrent pancreatitis. Emergent surgery has no benefit without cholangitis or obstruction. Gallstones are a leading cause of the disease, so removal is key.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man undergoing appendectomy under general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine develops a temperature of 39.8 C, an end-tidal carbon dioxide rising to 78 mm Hg, masseter rigidity, and a heart rate of 142. Arterial blood gas shows mixed acidosis and potassium of 6.2 mEq per liter. After stopping the volatile agent and hyperventilating with 100 percent oxygen, which drug is the most appropriate next step?
options: Intravenous calcium chloride alone
Intravenous propofol infusion to deepen the anesthetic and suppress muscle activity
Intravenous dantrolene, repeated until the signs resolve
Intravenous esmolol to slow the heart rate
items.explanation: Rising end-tidal carbon dioxide, rigidity, hyperthermia, and hyperkalemia after a volatile agent and succinylcholine indicate malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic crisis from uncontrolled calcium release in skeletal muscle. Dantrolene blocks the ryanodine receptor and is the specific treatment. Calcium and esmolol treat single features without stopping the process. Propofol is safe in this setting but does not reverse the crisis.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has a rapidly enlarging, mobile, 6 cm breast mass over four months. Core needle biopsy shows a cellular stroma with leaf-like architecture and mild atypia. Axillary examination is normal. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Simple enucleation of the mass through a small incision
Mastectomy with routine axillary node dissection
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by lumpectomy
Wide local excision with a margin of at least 1 cm and no axillary dissection
items.explanation: A rapidly growing mass with leaf-like stroma on biopsy suggests phyllodes tumor, which recurs locally if shelled out. Wide excision with clear margins is the standard, and mastectomy is used when margins cannot be achieved without poor cosmesis. Nodal spread is rare, so axillary dissection is not indicated. Chemotherapy has no established role in the initial management.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with severe malnutrition after prolonged bowel obstruction begins parenteral nutrition at full goal on hospital day three. Two days later she is weak and short of breath with new confusion. Which laboratory abnormality is the hallmark of this complication?
options: Hyperphosphatemia from impaired renal excretion
Hypophosphatemia from intracellular shift driven by insulin release
Hypernatremia from excess free water loss
Hypercalcemia from mobilization of bone mineral
items.explanation: Refeeding syndrome follows reintroduction of carbohydrate in a starved patient. Insulin surges drive phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, and thiamine is consumed. Hypophosphatemia causes weakness, respiratory failure, and confusion. Prevention is slow advancement of calories, replacement of electrolytes, and thiamine before feeding. The opposite abnormalities named here are not features of the syndrome. Cardiac and respiratory failure can follow if it is missed.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man has a 1.8 mm thick melanoma of the back with ulceration. There are no palpable nodes and no distant disease on staging. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Wide excision with 2 cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy
Wide excision with 1 cm margins and no nodal evaluation
Wide excision with 3 cm margins and elective lymph node dissection
Wide excision with 5 mm margins followed by interferon
items.explanation: Margin recommendations follow Breslow thickness: 1 cm for lesions up to 1 mm, 1 to 2 cm for 1 to 2 mm, and 2 cm for thicker lesions. Sentinel node biopsy is offered for lesions above 1 mm, and for thinner ones with adverse features, because nodal status is the strongest prognostic factor. Elective dissection of clinically negative nodes is not required.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetes presents with severe pain in the left thigh that is out of proportion to examination. He is febrile with a heart rate of 126 and blood pressure of 92/58 mm Hg. The skin is dusky with early bullae and crepitus, and white blood cell count is markedly elevated. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Computed tomography to define the extent before any intervention
Broad-spectrum antibiotics with immediate operative debridement
Intravenous antibiotics with repeat examination in twelve hours
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy before operation
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion, bullae, crepitus, and systemic toxicity indicate necrotizing soft tissue infection, a surgical emergency in which survival depends on speed of debridement. Broad-spectrum coverage including anaerobes and a protein synthesis inhibitor is given at the same time. Imaging, observation, and hyperbaric oxygen all delay source control and are never substitutes for operation.

items.stem: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking his anticoagulant has sudden pain, pallor, and coldness of the right leg for three hours. He has decreased sensation of the foot and mild weakness of the toes, and no arterial Doppler signal is audible in the foot. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
options: Elective angiography within the next several days to plan a staged revascularization
Observation with warming and elevation of the limb
Immediate primary amputation below the knee
Systemic anticoagulation followed by urgent revascularization
items.explanation: Acute embolic limb ischemia with sensory loss, motor weakness, and absent Doppler signals is a threatened limb, category IIb, that needs prompt revascularization. Anticoagulation is started at once to prevent propagation, then embolectomy or catheter-directed therapy restores flow. Delay beyond hours risks irreversible muscle necrosis. Amputation is for nonviable limbs, and warming does not restore perfusion.

items.stem: A 10-day-old boy has sudden bilious vomiting and abdominal distention. He is pale and lethargic with a heart rate of 190. Abdominal radiograph shows a paucity of distal gas. Which study should be obtained first in the stable resuscitated infant, and what does it show?
options: Contrast barium enema showing a microcolon with a rectosigmoid transition zone between narrow and dilated colon
Abdominal ultrasound showing a thickened pyloric muscle
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study showing the duodenojejunal junction right of midline
Plain film showing a double bubble with distal gas
items.explanation: Bilious emesis in a newborn is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise. The contrast study shows an abnormally positioned duodenojejunal junction, often with a corkscrew duodenum. An unstable infant goes directly to the operating room for the Ladd procedure. A microcolon points to ileal atresia, a thickened pylorus causes nonbilious vomiting, and a double bubble with distal gas suggests partial duodenal obstruction.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a severe burn covering about 40 percent of her body surface area is 8 hours from injury. Urine output is 20 mL per hour. What is the best adjustment to resuscitation?
options: Increase lactated Ringer and titrate hourly to urine output
Stop fluids because pulmonary edema is inevitable in burns
Switch to a hypotonic dextrose solution for the second day
Give a large colloid bolus and a diuretic to raise urine output
items.explanation: Burn shock resuscitation uses a crystalloid formula as a starting estimate, then the infusion is titrated hourly to urine output of about 0.5 mL per kilogram per hour for adults. Low output means under-resuscitation, so the rate rises. Stopping fluids risks renal failure. Hypotonic dextrose causes hyponatremia and does not restore volume. Diuretics worsen intravascular depletion and cannot be used to mask hypovolemia.

items.stem: A 74-year-old man has had several months of dysphagia for solids, regurgitation of undigested food hours after meals, halitosis, and a gurgling sound in the neck. A barium swallow shows a posterior outpouching at the pharyngoesophageal junction. Which anatomic feature explains this condition?
options: Herniation of the gastric cardia through the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm into the posterior mediastinum
Failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax during swallowing
Herniation of mucosa through the triangle between the oblique and transverse cricopharyngeal fibers
Traction from adjacent inflamed mediastinal lymph nodes
items.explanation: Zenker diverticulum is a pulsion pseudodiverticulum that forms through Killian triangle, a weak area above the cricopharyngeus muscle, from incoordination and high pressure during swallowing. Regurgitation of old food and a neck gurgle are typical. Hiatal herniation is a different disorder, failed sphincter relaxation describes achalasia, and traction diverticula occur in the mid esophagus. Treatment is cricopharyngeal myotomy with diverticulectomy or endoscopic septotomy.

items.stem: A 30-year-old man has abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea. Colonoscopy shows continuous inflammation from the rectum to the splenic flexure with a loss of vascular pattern and no skip areas. Which histologic feature supports ulcerative colitis over Crohn disease?
options: Mucosal inflammation with crypt abscesses and no granulomas
Transmural inflammation with noncaseating granulomas in the wall
Deep fissuring ulcers with fat wrapping of the bowel
Patchy inflammation with preserved rectal mucosa
items.explanation: Ulcerative colitis is a continuous mucosal disease beginning at the rectum, with crypt abscesses, crypt distortion, and inflammation confined to the mucosa and superficial submucosa. Transmural inflammation, granulomas, fissures, creeping fat, and rectal sparing are typical of Crohn disease. Total proctocolectomy is curative for ulcerative colitis but not for Crohn disease, which recurs, so the distinction guides surgical decisions.

items.stem: A 25-year-old woman has left upper quadrant pain and a platelet count of 12,000 per microliter with a normal hemoglobin and white cell count. Platelet counts have remained low despite corticosteroids and immunoglobulin. What is the next best option?
options: Splenic artery embolization as the preferred option
Long-term high-dose prednisone as the only therapy
Platelet transfusions every week on a scheduled basis
Splenectomy after vaccination against encapsulated organisms
items.explanation: Immune thrombocytopenia refractory to first-line corticosteroids and immunoglobulin is treated with second-line options, and splenectomy offers durable remission for most patients by removing the site of platelet destruction. Vaccines against pneumococcus, meningococcus, and Haemophilus influenzae are given beforehand. Embolization is a less established alternative. Prolonged high-dose steroids cause toxicity, and scheduled transfusions are destroyed quickly and are reserved for bleeding.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man needs elective colectomy for a large polyp. He received a drug-eluting coronary stent seven months ago for stable angina and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He has no recent symptoms. How should his antiplatelet therapy be managed perioperatively?
options: Stop both agents a week before surgery to minimize bleeding
Continue aspirin and hold clopidogrel about five to seven days before surgery
Continue both agents without interruption through the operation
Postpone the operation for another full year while both antiplatelet agents continue unchanged
items.explanation: After elective stenting, dual therapy is needed for several months, and surgery beyond that window is acceptable. Aspirin is continued to protect the stent, while the second agent is held to reduce bleeding and resumed soon after. Stopping both raises the risk of stent thrombosis. Continuing both is reserved for urgent surgery within the vulnerable period. Delay for a year is not needed.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman has a firm thyroid nodule and elevated calcitonin. Her father died of thyroid cancer and a brother had hypertension from an adrenal tumor. Fine needle biopsy suggests medullary carcinoma. Before thyroidectomy, which evaluation is the most important?
options: Radioactive iodine uptake scan
Thyroglobulin level with antibody testing
Serum cortisol after dexamethasone
Plasma metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma
items.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma in a family with adrenal tumors suggests multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 with a RET mutation. A coexisting pheochromocytoma must be excluded and treated first, with alpha blockade, because anesthesia or operation can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. The tumor arises from C cells, so iodine uptake and thyroglobulin are unhelpful, and cortisol testing addresses a different problem.

items.stem: A 56-year-old man has a pancreatic fistula draining 900 mL daily after distal pancreatectomy. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16 mEq per liter, and chloride 112 mEq per liter. The calculated anion gap is 11. Which mechanism best explains the acid-base disturbance?
options: Loss of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid causing a normal anion gap acidosis
Accumulation of lactate from tissue hypoperfusion
Accumulation of ketoacids from prolonged starvation and inadequate carbohydrate intake
Retention of acid from renal failure
items.explanation: Pancreatic and small bowel secretions contain high concentrations of bicarbonate, so large fistula losses cause a hyperchloremic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis as chloride rises to replace lost bicarbonate. Lactic acidosis, ketoacidosis, and renal failure all add unmeasured anions and raise the gap. Treatment is replacement of volume with a bicarbonate-containing balanced solution and control of the fistula.

items.stem: A 78-year-old woman has a rapidly growing, painless, violaceous nodule on the cheek that has doubled in size in six weeks. Biopsy shows small round blue cells that stain positive for cytokeratin 20 in a perinuclear dot pattern. What is the most appropriate management of the primary lesion after staging?
options: Excision with narrow 1 mm margins, no nodal evaluation, and routine clinical follow-up every year
Wide local excision with sentinel lymph node biopsy, then consideration of adjuvant radiation
Topical immunotherapy applied for several weeks
Systemic chemotherapy alone with no resection
items.explanation: The rapid growth, small round blue cell histology, and dot-like cytokeratin 20 staining indicate Merkel cell carcinoma, an aggressive neuroendocrine skin cancer. Treatment is wide excision with sentinel node evaluation because occult nodal spread is common, usually followed by radiation to the primary site and nodal basin. Narrow excision without staging misses spread, and topical therapy or chemotherapy alone is inadequate.

items.stem: A 33-year-old man with a known bleeding disorder has epistaxis and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. He needs elective hernia repair. Laboratory studies show a mildly prolonged partial thromboplastin time and low von Willebrand factor activity with normal platelet count. Which perioperative therapy is most appropriate for a mild type 1 form?
options: Platelet transfusion immediately before incision
Vitamin K infusion the evening before surgery
Desmopressin before the procedure to release stored von Willebrand factor
Cryoprecipitate only after bleeding begins
items.explanation: In mild type 1 von Willebrand disease, desmopressin raises factor levels by releasing endothelial stores and is first-line before minor procedures. Factor concentrate is used for major surgery or poor response. Platelets are normal in number, vitamin K treats deficiencies of vitamin K dependent factors, and waiting for bleeding to start abandons prophylaxis. Antifibrinolytic agents are a useful adjunct.

items.stem: Six weeks after kidney transplantation, a 45-year-old man on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone has tremor, hyperkalemia, hypertension, and a rising creatinine. Biopsy shows no inflammatory infiltrate but isometric vacuolization of tubular cells. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
options: Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, treated by lowering the tacrolimus dose guided by trough levels
Acute cellular rejection, treated with higher tacrolimus troughs and immediate pulse corticosteroid therapy
Hyperacute rejection, treated with graft removal
Cytomegalovirus infection, treated with mycophenolate escalation
items.explanation: Tremor, hyperkalemia, hypertension, and tubular vacuolization without lymphocytic infiltrate point to calcineurin inhibitor toxicity, which is dose related. Trough levels guide reduction. Acute cellular rejection shows interstitial inflammation, and hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours from preformed antibodies. Increasing immunosuppression for infection is wrong and could worsen the viral disease. The biopsy is the key discriminator.

items.stem: A 14-year-old boy awakens with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomiting. The testis is high-riding with a horizontal lie, and the cremasteric reflex is absent. Pain began three hours ago, and there is no fever. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Scrotal ultrasound with a repeat examination tomorrow
Antibiotics for epididymitis for ten days
Manual detorsion at the bedside followed by outpatient follow-up in the clinic
Immediate surgical exploration with detorsion and bilateral orchiopexy
items.explanation: Acute testicular pain with a high-riding horizontal testis and absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent is torsion until proven otherwise, and salvage rates fall sharply after about six hours. Surgery should not be delayed for imaging when suspicion is high. Both testes are fixed because the anatomic defect is usually bilateral. Antibiotics treat epididymitis, and manual reduction alone is unreliable.

items.stem: A 36-year-old man is in the intensive care unit after massive resuscitation for a ruptured spleen and liver laceration. Peak airway pressures have risen, urine output has fallen to 10 mL per hour, and the abdomen is tense and distended. Bladder pressure is 28 mm Hg, and lactate is rising. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Additional crystalloid bolus to improve renal perfusion
Decompressive laparotomy with temporary abdominal closure
Furosemide infusion to promote diuresis
Continued observation with serial bladder pressure checks
items.explanation: A sustained bladder pressure above 20 mm Hg with new organ dysfunction defines abdominal compartment syndrome. Elevated intra-abdominal pressure compresses the vena cava, raises airway pressure, and reduces renal flow. When medical measures fail or the patient is deteriorating, decompressive laparotomy is the definitive treatment. More fluid worsens edema, diuretics do not relieve the pressure, and waiting risks irreversible injury.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman has progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids, nocturnal regurgitation, and weight loss. Barium esophagram shows a dilated esophagus tapering to a smooth narrow segment at the gastroesophageal junction. High-resolution manometry would most likely show which pattern?
options: Normal sphincter relaxation with high-amplitude, repetitive peristaltic contractions of the distal esophagus
Hypotensive sphincter with preserved peristalsis
Incomplete relaxation of the lower sphincter with absent peristalsis
Simultaneous contractions with normal sphincter relaxation
items.explanation: A bird beak tapering and a dilated esophagus suggest achalasia, in which loss of inhibitory neurons produces incomplete sphincter relaxation and absent peristalsis. Treatment options are pneumatic dilation, laparoscopic Heller myotomy with partial fundoplication, or peroral endoscopic myotomy. Hypotensive sphincter suggests reflux, and simultaneous contractions with normal relaxation describe distal esophageal spasm. Endoscopy first excludes a malignant cause of the narrowing.

items.stem: An 81-year-old nursing home resident has three days of progressive abdominal distention and obstipation. An abdominal radiograph shows a massively dilated sigmoid loop shaped like a coffee bean with its apex in the right upper quadrant. He is afebrile and has no peritonitis. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Immediate emergency sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy
Contrast barium enema to confirm the diagnosis before any decompression is attempted
Nasogastric decompression and observation alone
Flexible sigmoidoscopic detorsion with rectal tube placement
items.explanation: The coffee bean sign with obstipation indicates sigmoid volvulus. Without ischemia or peritonitis, endoscopic detorsion succeeds in most patients and relieves obstruction safely. Because recurrence is common, an elective sigmoid resection is planned during the same admission for fit patients. Emergency resection is reserved for gangrene, perforation, or failed decompression. Contrast study adds delay and risk, and observation alone does not untwist the bowel.

items.stem: A 29-year-old woman who has used oral contraceptives for eight years presents with sudden right upper quadrant pain and hypotension. Computed tomography shows a 7 cm hepatic lesion with intratumoral hemorrhage and free blood around the liver. After resuscitation she is stabilized. What is the best management of the underlying lesion?
options: Hepatic resection or embolization, with cessation of hormonal therapy
Observation with repeat imaging in six months
Percutaneous needle biopsy and continued hormonal therapy
Systemic chemotherapy for presumed hepatocellular carcinoma with palliative intent
items.explanation: A large hepatic adenoma with hemorrhage in a woman using estrogen-containing contraception is the classic scenario. Adenomas over 5 cm carry risk of bleeding and malignant transformation, so resection is advised, and embolization controls acute bleeding. Estrogen exposure is stopped. Observation suits small lesions, biopsy risks further hemorrhage, and chemotherapy is unwarranted without evidence of carcinoma.

items.stem: A 55-year-old woman undergoing a nerve block for shoulder surgery suddenly develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, a metallic taste, and then a generalized seizure, followed by wide-complex bradycardia. A large dose of bupivacaine was injected. In addition to airway support and seizure control, which treatment is specifically indicated?
options: Intravenous lidocaine to suppress the arrhythmia
Intravenous calcium gluconate bolus
Intravenous lipid emulsion
Intravenous naloxone infusion
items.explanation: Central nervous system excitation followed by cardiovascular collapse after a regional block indicates local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Lipid emulsion acts as a sink that pulls the drug from tissue, and reduced epinephrine doses are used during arrest. Lidocaine is another local anesthetic and worsens the toxicity. Calcium is for hyperkalemia and calcium channel blocker overdose, and naloxone reverses opioids only.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a calcium of 11.4 mg/dL on routine testing, with elevated parathyroid hormone, a 24-hour urine calcium of 380 mg, and a T-score of minus 2.8 at the forearm. She has no symptoms. Which finding is the strongest indication for parathyroidectomy?
options: Calcium only mildly above the upper limit of normal
Osteoporosis, which meets guideline criteria even in asymptomatic disease
Age above 50 years alone, regardless of calcium and bone findings in the patient
A normal serum creatinine level
items.explanation: Asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism is treated surgically when calcium is more than 1 mg/dL above normal, bone density T-score is at or below minus 2.5, a vertebral fracture exists, creatinine clearance is below 60, kidney stones are present, or age is under 50. Osteoporosis alone qualifies. Mildly elevated calcium, an older age, and normal renal function do not by themselves establish an indication.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman has an enlarging 9 cm high-grade soft tissue sarcoma of the anterior thigh. Biopsy confirms undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, and imaging shows no metastases or major neurovascular involvement. Which treatment strategy gives the best chance of limb preservation with local control?
options: Primary amputation at the hip for all large tumors
Enucleation through the pseudocapsule alone
Limb-sparing wide resection combined with radiation therapy
Isolated chemotherapy without resection
items.explanation: Most extremity sarcomas are treated with limb-sparing wide excision plus radiation, delivered before or after surgery, which gives local control equal to amputation. Enucleation through the pseudocapsule leaves tumor cells and recurs. Amputation is reserved for tumors involving neurovascular structures that cannot be spared. Chemotherapy is selectively used and does not replace resection. Amputation is now uncommon in modern practice.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes into transfusion of red cells for postoperative anemia, a 60-year-old woman develops fever, chills, flank pain, and hypotension. Urine becomes red-brown. Which action should be taken first?
options: Stop the transfusion and keep intravenous access with saline
Slow the transfusion rate and give an antihistamine
Complete the unit while giving acetaminophen
Send the blood bag to the laboratory before changing anything
items.explanation: Fever, flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine suggest acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility, usually due to clerical error. The first step is to stop the transfusion immediately, maintain access, and support blood pressure and urine output, then verify identification and notify the blood bank. Slowing or completing the unit, or treating symptoms alone, continues the exposure and worsens hemolysis and renal injury.

items.stem: A 9-year-old boy is struck on the right side of the head by a baseball and briefly loses consciousness. He seems fine for two hours, then becomes drowsy with vomiting and a dilated right pupil. Computed tomography shows a biconvex, lens-shaped hyperdense collection. What is the most likely source of bleeding?
options: Bridging cortical veins stretched between brain and dura
Middle meningeal artery injury beneath a temporal skull fracture
Rupture of a berry aneurysm at the circle of Willis
Diffuse axonal injury with shearing of white matter
items.explanation: A lucid interval followed by deterioration and a lens-shaped extra-axial collection that does not cross sutures indicates epidural hematoma, usually from the middle meningeal artery after temporal bone fracture. The expanding clot causes uncal herniation, producing an ipsilateral dilated pupil, and requires urgent craniotomy. Subdural hematoma arises from bridging veins, and aneurysmal bleeding is subarachnoid.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with severe aspiration pneumonia is intubated. Her arterial oxygen to inspired oxygen ratio is 90, and chest imaging shows bilateral opacities with normal cardiac function. Which intervention has the strongest mortality evidence in this condition?
options: High tidal volume ventilation to normalize carbon dioxide and maximize alveolar recruitment
Aggressive diuresis targeting negative balance of several liters
Routine pulmonary artery catheter placement
Low tidal volume ventilation with prone positioning for long daily periods
items.explanation: Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome is treated with lung protective ventilation at about 6 mL per kilogram of predicted body weight with plateau pressure limited, and prone positioning for most of the day improves survival when the oxygen ratio is below about 150. High volumes cause ventilator injury, and catheters add risk without benefit. Fluid is managed conservatively once shock resolves, not aggressively.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has melena and a 5 cm submucosal gastric mass with a central ulcer found at endoscopy. Biopsy shows spindle cells staining positive for CD117 and DOG1. Computed tomography shows no metastases. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Subtotal gastrectomy with extended lymph node dissection
Complete surgical resection with negative margins and no lymphadenectomy
Chemotherapy with a platinum regimen before any surgery
Endoscopic surveillance every year
items.explanation: Spindle cells positive for CD117 and DOG1 define a gastrointestinal stromal tumor. Resectable disease is removed completely, usually by wedge resection, because nodal spread is rare and lymphadenectomy adds nothing. Adjuvant imatinib is considered based on size, mitotic rate, and location. These tumors are resistant to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy, and surveillance alone is inappropriate for a bleeding tumor of this size.

items.stem: A 58-year-old man has a rectal adenocarcinoma 6 cm from the anal verge.
