Magnetic resonance imaging shows invasion through the muscularis propria with two enlarged mesorectal nodes and a threatened circumferential margin. No distant disease is found. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Neoadjuvant chemoradiation or total neoadjuvant therapy, then total mesorectal excision
Upfront low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, followed by clinical observation only
Transanal local excision alone
Palliative diverting colostomy without further therapy
items.explanation: Locally advanced mid rectal cancer, meaning stage II or III disease, is treated with neoadjuvant therapy to downstage the tumor, improve margin clearance, and reduce local recurrence, followed by total mesorectal excision. Upfront surgery risks positive margins when the margin is threatened. Local excision is for small early lesions, and palliation is inappropriate for curable disease.

items.stem: A 4-year-old girl has recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and jaundice. Ultrasound and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography show fusiform dilation of the common bile duct to 3 cm without intrahepatic involvement. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Cyst enterostomy with internal drainage only
Endoscopic sphincterotomy with long-term biliary stent placement and periodic exchange
Observation with annual imaging until adulthood
Complete cyst excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy
items.explanation: A fusiform extrahepatic dilation is a type I choledochal cyst. Because the lining carries lifelong risk of cholangiocarcinoma, the standard is complete excision of the cyst with biliary reconstruction by hepaticojejunostomy. Internal drainage leaves the cyst wall and its malignant potential. Endoscopic therapy does not remove the cyst, and observation permits cholangitis and later cancer.

items.stem: A 70-year-old woman is extubated after cholecystectomy under rocuronium. In recovery she has rapid shallow breathing, cannot lift her head, and has a train-of-four showing fade with only two twitches. Oxygen saturation is falling. Which agent best reverses the blockade?
options: Neostigmine given alone without an antimuscarinic agent to counteract the bradycardia
Atropine given alone to increase acetylcholine
Sugammadex, which encapsulates the steroidal neuromuscular blocking agent
Flumazenil to antagonize residual sedation
items.explanation: Residual paralysis after a steroidal blocker presents with weak respiratory effort and fade on train-of-four monitoring. Sugammadex binds rocuronium directly and reverses even deep blockade quickly. Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase and needs a concurrent antimuscarinic to blunt bradycardia and secretions. Atropine alone does not reverse paralysis, and flumazenil antagonizes benzodiazepines, not neuromuscular blockers. Quantitative train-of-four monitoring confirms recovery before extubation.

items.stem: A 55-year-old man has a 4 cm right adrenal mass found on imaging for abdominal pain. Unenhanced attenuation is 35 Hounsfield units. He is hypertensive and has mild hypokalemia. Which set of biochemical tests is most appropriate before deciding on adrenalectomy?
options: Serum calcitonin and thyroglobulin with thyroid ultrasound and fine needle aspiration of the adrenal mass
Plasma metanephrines, overnight dexamethasone suppression, and aldosterone to renin ratio
Urinary five-hydroxyindoleacetic acid and chromogranin
Serum amylase and lipase
items.explanation: Every adrenal incidentaloma needs evaluation for function: pheochromocytoma by metanephrines, autonomous cortisol secretion by dexamethasone suppression, and primary aldosteronism by aldosterone to renin ratio when hypertension or hypokalemia is present. Operation is considered for functioning tumors or those with suspicious imaging features. The other tests relate to thyroid, carcinoid, and pancreatic disease. Tumor size and imaging features then guide the decision for surgery.

items.stem: A 66-year-old farmer has a 1.5 cm pearly, ulcerated nodule on the nasal ala. Biopsy shows basal cell carcinoma with an infiltrative growth pattern. Which treatment offers the highest cure rate while preserving tissue?
options: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen
Standard excision with 1 mm margins
Topical imiquimod cream
Mohs micrographic surgery
items.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma on the central face with an infiltrative histologic pattern is a high-risk tumor, and Mohs surgery with complete margin examination gives the best cure rate while sparing normal tissue in cosmetically sensitive areas. Cryotherapy and topical treatments suit superficial low-risk lesions. Narrow standard margins carry a higher rate of positive margins for infiltrative tumors.

items.stem: A 29-year-old driver is evaluated after a high-speed head-on collision. Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum, and computed tomography angiography shows an intimal tear with a small pseudoaneurysm just distal to the left subclavian artery. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Impulse control with beta-blockade, followed by early thoracic endovascular repair
Immediate median sternotomy with cardiopulmonary bypass
Vasodilator infusion to lower afterload alone
Repeat imaging in one year without treatment
items.explanation: Blunt aortic injury at the isthmus involves a partial-thickness tear contained by adventitia. Heart rate and pressure are lowered to reduce shear forces while repair is planned, and endovascular stent graft repair is preferred over open repair for most anatomies. Sternotomy accesses the ascending aorta, not the isthmus. Vasodilators alone increase shear by raising the rate of pressure rise, and observation risks rupture.

items.stem: A 50-year-old woman who had a Billroth II reconstruction for ulcer disease reports that fifteen minutes after meals she has palpitations, sweating, cramping, and diarrhea. A late episode of weakness and tremor appears two hours after eating. What is the best initial management?
options: Immediate conversion to a total gastrectomy with Roux-en-Y esophagojejunostomy reconstruction
Intravenous antibiotics for bacterial overgrowth
Dietary modification with small low-carbohydrate meals and separating liquids from solids
Prokinetic agents to speed gastric emptying
items.explanation: Early dumping from rapid entry of hyperosmolar chyme into the small bowel, and late dumping from reactive hypoglycemia, are managed first with diet: small frequent meals, less simple sugar, protein and fiber, and fluids between meals. Acarbose or octreotide are next if symptoms persist, and reconstruction is a last resort. Prokinetics accelerate emptying and worsen symptoms.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man is diagnosed with colon cancer. His mother had endometrial cancer at age 45, and his maternal uncle had colon cancer at age 42. Tumor testing shows loss of staining for MLH1 and PMS2 with a negative BRAF mutation. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The tumor is sporadic because of the age at presentation and needs no genetic counseling or family screening
A germline mismatch repair mutation is likely, and extended or total colectomy should be discussed
Genetic testing is required only if polyps number over 100
Prophylactic proctocolectomy is mandatory for all patients
items.explanation: The family history and loss of mismatch repair proteins without the BRAF mutation point to Lynch syndrome, the most common hereditary colorectal cancer syndrome. Germline testing confirms it, and surgical options include extended resection because of the high metachronous cancer risk. Surveillance for endometrial and other cancers follows. Polyp counts above 100 define polyposis, and mandatory proctocolectomy is not indicated.

items.stem: A 71-year-old woman has fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain. Her blood pressure is 84/50 mm Hg, and she is confused. Ultrasound shows a dilated common bile duct with stones. Bilirubin is 6.4 mg/dL and white blood cell count is 21,000. After fluids and antibiotics, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the next scheduled list
Observation until the fever resolves
Urgent biliary decompression by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography
Magnetic resonance imaging before any intervention
items.explanation: Fever, jaundice, pain, hypotension, and confusion constitute Reynolds pentad, a severe suppurative cholangitis that carries high mortality unless the obstructed system is drained promptly. Endoscopic drainage is the preferred method, with percutaneous drainage as an alternative, and definitive stone management follows after recovery. Cholecystectomy does not decompress the duct, waiting is dangerous, and imaging should not delay drainage.

items.stem: A 37-year-old woman has a 2.8 cm solitary thyroid nodule. Fine needle aspiration is reported as follicular neoplasm, and thyroid stimulating hormone is normal. Ultrasound shows no suspicious nodes. Which management is most appropriate?
options: Diagnostic thyroid lobectomy
Repeat aspiration in five years
Total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection
Radioactive iodine ablation before any surgery
items.explanation: A follicular neoplasm diagnosis cannot separate adenoma from carcinoma on cytology because carcinoma requires proof of capsular or vascular invasion on the whole specimen. Diagnostic lobectomy provides the answer and, if benign, avoids lifelong hormone replacement. Total thyroidectomy is chosen for large nodules, bilateral disease, or patient preference. Iodine ablation has no role before diagnosis.

items.stem: A 34-year-old man has 40 percent total body surface area partial and full thickness flame burns, weighs 80 kg, and arrives two hours after injury. Using the modified Brooke or Parkland approach, which initial fluid plan is most appropriate?
options: A fixed maintenance rate of 100 mL per hour of dextrose solution
Colloid infusion only until the burn wounds are covered
Repeated large boluses of hypertonic saline in the first hour to restore circulating volume while monitoring sodium
Lactated Ringer solution at a calculated rate, adjusted hourly to urine output near 0.5 mL per kg per hour
items.explanation: Burn resuscitation uses balanced crystalloid with an initial estimate of about 2 to 4 mL per kilogram per percentage of burned surface over twenty-four hours, half in the first eight hours from injury. Rates are titrated hourly to urine output because formulas are only a starting point. Fixed maintenance rates underresuscitate, colloid is not first-line, and hypertonic boluses risk hypernatremia.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man with long-standing reflux has Barrett esophagus. Surveillance biopsies from a nodule-free segment show high-grade dysplasia confirmed by two expert pathologists. Which treatment is most appropriate?
options: Repeat endoscopy in three years
Endoscopic eradication with radiofrequency ablation and resection of visible lesions
High-dose acid suppression alone with no ablation
Immediate transhiatal esophagectomy in every case regardless of fitness or lesion size
items.explanation: High-grade dysplasia in Barrett esophagus carries substantial risk of progression to adenocarcinoma. Endoscopic eradication, with mucosal resection of nodules followed by radiofrequency ablation of the remaining metaplasia, is the preferred treatment, with high success and lower morbidity than esophagectomy. Acid suppression does not remove dysplasia, and long surveillance intervals are only appropriate for nondysplastic disease.

items.stem: A 62-year-old man has left lower quadrant pain, fever, and a white blood cell count of 17,000. Computed tomography shows sigmoid diverticulitis with a 5 cm pericolic abscess and no free air. He is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Emergency Hartmann procedure for all abscesses
Oral antibiotics and early discharge without drainage
Antibiotics with percutaneous image-guided drainage
Colonoscopy the same day to look for a source
items.explanation: A diverticular abscess larger than about 3 to 4 cm is treated with antibiotics and percutaneous drainage, which controls sepsis and often allows a later elective single-stage resection. Emergency resection is reserved for failure of drainage or generalized peritonitis. Small abscesses may resolve with antibiotics alone. Colonoscopy during acute inflammation risks perforation and is delayed several weeks.

items.stem: A 66-year-old man has an incidental 2.5 cm cystic pancreatic lesion communicating with a dilated main pancreatic duct measuring 9 mm. Endoscopic ultrasound shows a mural nodule. Which management is most appropriate for this branch and main duct intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm?
options: Surgical resection of the involved pancreas
Repeat imaging in five years
Percutaneous drainage of the cyst
Octreotide therapy to shrink the cyst
items.explanation: A main pancreatic duct measuring 5 to 9 mm is a worrisome feature, and a duct of 10 mm or more, an enhancing mural nodule, or jaundice are high-risk features that warrant resection in fit patients because of the risk of invasive carcinoma. Surveillance suits low-risk branch duct lesions. Drainage and octreotide do not remove the neoplastic epithelium or its malignant potential.

items.stem: A 40-year-old woman falls from a ladder and has an unstable pelvic ring injury. Blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg despite two units of blood. Extended ultrasound examination of the abdomen is negative for free fluid, and a pelvic binder is already in place. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnostic laparotomy to explore for intraperitoneal bleeding
Removal of the binder to examine the perineum
Preperitoneal pelvic packing or angioembolization with ongoing transfusion
Large-volume crystalloid infusion until blood pressure and urine output fully normalize
items.explanation: Unstable pelvic fracture with a negative abdominal ultrasound suggests retroperitoneal venous or bony bleeding. After binder placement and balanced transfusion, hemorrhage control comes from preperitoneal packing, often with external fixation, or from angioembolization when arterial bleeding is suspected. Laparotomy without intraperitoneal blood releases tamponade, and crystalloid worsens coagulopathy. Balanced transfusion with early tranexamic acid supports clotting.

items.stem: A 75-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation has sudden severe periumbilical pain with minimal tenderness, vomiting, and bloody diarrhea. Lactate is 4.6. Computed tomography angiography shows a filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery distal to the middle colic origin. What is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Observation with bowel rest, nasogastric decompression, and broad-spectrum antibiotics only
Elective colonoscopy within one week
Intravenous vasodilator infusion alone
Anticoagulation and laparotomy with embolectomy and resection of nonviable bowel
items.explanation: Pain out of proportion to tenderness in a patient with atrial fibrillation and an arterial filling defect indicates acute embolic mesenteric ischemia. Prompt systemic anticoagulation, revascularization by embolectomy or endovascular means, and resection of nonviable bowel with second-look assessment are required. Delay risks transmural necrosis. Bowel rest alone or colonoscopy is inadequate, and vasodilators are for nonocclusive disease.

items.stem: A 77-year-old man on antibiotics for pneumonia has profuse watery diarrhea, abdominal distention, hypotension, fever, and a white blood cell count of 32,000. Toxin testing is positive, and radiography shows a dilated colon. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Oral vancomycin with intravenous metronidazole, and surgical consultation for colectomy
Oral metronidazole alone, continued for two weeks with close monitoring of the white cell count
Loperamide for symptom control
Stopping antibiotics with no specific therapy
items.explanation: Hypotension, ileus, megacolon, and marked leukocytosis define fulminant Clostridioides difficile colitis. Treatment is high-dose oral vancomycin, with intravenous metronidazole when ileus limits delivery, and early surgical input because failure of medical therapy requires subtotal colectomy or diverting ileostomy with lavage. Antimotility drugs risk megacolon, and monotherapy with metronidazole is inadequate. Fecal microbiota transplantation is reserved for recurrent disease and is not an emergency measure.

items.stem: A 24-year-old man undergoes splenectomy for a grade V splenic injury after blunt trauma. Which plan best reduces his lifelong risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy infection?
options: Daily oral penicillin prophylaxis taken for life without any vaccination against encapsulated organisms and no patient education
Annual splenic scan to check for regrowth
No intervention because the risk is negligible in adults
Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination, with patient education about fever
items.explanation: Loss of the spleen impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae. Vaccination against all three, ideally two weeks after surgery when done after trauma, plus early antibiotics and urgent evaluation for fever, forms the standard strategy. Prophylactic antibiotics alone are insufficient, and the risk persists for life in adults.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with cirrhosis from chronic viral hepatitis presents with hematemesis and a heart rate of 118. Endoscopy shows bleeding esophageal varices treated successfully with band ligation. Which additional medical therapy should accompany the procedure?
options: High-dose intravenous proton pump inhibitor infusion continued alone for several days after the banding
Vasoactive infusion such as octreotide and prophylactic antibiotics such as ceftriaxone
Aggressive transfusion to a hemoglobin of 12 g/dL
Vitamin K infusion as the sole treatment
items.explanation: Variceal hemorrhage is managed with resuscitation using a restrictive transfusion threshold near 7 g/dL, a splanchnic vasoconstrictor to lower portal pressure, endoscopic band ligation, and short-course antibiotic prophylaxis, which reduces infection and mortality. Overtransfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding. Acid suppression does not control variceal bleeding, and vitamin K does not address it. Early endoscopy within twelve hours is standard once resuscitated.
